content:
In the past few days, two separate reports have pointed to different ways Apple could boost its profits by growing its services revenue.

I believe Apple absolutely should do the first of these — but not the second — and it appears Phil Schiller would agree…

Let me first summarise both reports.

Home security and monitoring services

On Friday, a Bloomberg report suggested Apple may be planning to launch an entirely new home security and monitoring service, expected to debut alongside several long-awaited new home hardware products.

Squeezing more revenue from the App Store

A second Bloomberg report on Sunday suggested Apple is looking at ways to squeeze more revenue and profit from the App Store.

Apple shouldn't do the latter

I believe, on the contrary, that the second approach would be a very serious mistake.

Apple's effective monopoly over iPhone app sales is already under scrutiny from regulators around the world. In most countries, if you want to sell iPhone apps, you have to go through the official App Store — there is no alternative, and you have to accept Apple's terms without any bargaining power.

I know many people feel that no one is forced to buy an iPhone or develop apps for one, but this view is inconsistent with how even the most laissez-faire capitalism actually works: even in the US, antitrust law has been around since 1890. Once you reach a certain level of market dominance, you are required to follow rules of conduct to ensure you don't abuse that position.

Trying to squeeze more money out of the App Store is the opposite of 'skating to where the puck is going' — and Schiller is reportedly in agreement. This is also cited as one of the reasons for him stepping back from frontline duties, according to Bloomberg.

Innovative services are the right direction

Apple should launch brand new, innovative services that customers are happy to pay for. I can easily imagine the value of Apple offering a home security monitoring service.

As I said back in 2024, developing its own smart home cameras would be one of the smartest moves the company could make. I made the same point about the long-rumoured Apple smart doorbell at the time. Layering optional service packages on top of security products makes a lot of sense, for two reasons.

First, all the privacy reasons I outlined before apply. HomeKit Secure Video has already done a great deal of work in protecting the privacy of security camera footage. If there is one company I would trust to run AI analysis on security camera footage, it is Apple.

Second, Apple is of course best placed to fully integrate security hardware and services within the HomeKit ecosystem. I firmly believe there are many other areas where Apple could offer similar advantages.

For me, the point is that Apple needs to treat services with the same attitude it brings to hardware — building great products that customers are happy and willing to pay for, rather than making money in ways that annoy customers, developers and regulators.

What do you think? Feel free to share your views in the comments.
